uniequip_002_jesca2:
Holding her grandpa's hand, she climbs her way up onto the luxurious bureau.
'Alright, Jess, now before we start drawing, remember, first we clean our hands. No cake crumbs, no cookie crumbs.'
'I did! What are we gonna draw, Grandpa?'
'Ooh... lookit here, I got a certificate, from when ol' Grandpa came back from the frontier. But they forgot to draw me a darn picture of the place. How about you help me fill that in, Jessica?'
'Uhh... I've never been to the frontier, though...'
'Your brother and your sisters went a whole bunch with your dad, didn't they? They ever tell you what was out there?'
'They said the frontier's got nothing, but also said it's all... 'ripe for the picking.' I heard that, Grandpa, 'ripe for the picking,' but how do I draw it? I'm kind of lost...'
'Aw, heck, they love to teach you some strange old words. Say, forget that, how about you draw something the likes of which they've never seen. I'll teach you. Remember how I told you of the Seven Bastards of the wastes, those catapulting Liberi robbers?'
'Oh, yeah, yeah!'
'Remember what that big ol' cactus was shaped like?'
'Huge in every direction, like a mangler!'
'Remember why tumbleweeds make a good wild bonfire?'
'They're brambly and thin and they catch with a spark!'
'Remember how to ride a burdenbeast?'
'Pull the reins tight and straddle that saddle!'
'Attagirl, Jessica. You always wanted to know more, see more, just like your brother and sisters? You ask me, I bet my bottom dollar you'll be just like them once you're as grown up as them, oh the things you'll know and see. But Grandpa's personal little tales, I've not yet told a soul but you, Jessica. They don't know 'em—heck, your dad doesn't know 'em.'
'Okay! When they come back, I'll tell them, then I'll show them my picture, and it's gonna blow their socks off! 'Wow, Jessica, you heard stories we never got to hear!''
......
She pulls the burdenbeast's reins, straddles the saddle, and unfolds an old sheet of paper in the light of the sinking sun.
Just about below the edge of the wastes, its last warm rays shine through the paper. A sheen, she might swear, casts over faded fountain ink.
The old man trots his burdenback alongside her. She yanks the reins tight, and settles back in her seat.
'What's that you're peeking at, Jessica?'
'It's... a picture, something I drew when I was real young, of the frontier.'
'You came out here as a kid? Never mentioned that.'
'No, I just had someone describe it to me. Held my hand while I was drawing.'
'Not half bad, all things considered. Hell of a 'canvas' too.'
'This is his certificate, the one who showed me how to draw it. He was my grandfather.'
'Your grandfather. A hero of the states?'
'Yeah... a hero of the states. And a hero of mine.'
uniequip_003_jesca2:
'Miss Jessica...'
She hid behind the sheriff, sizing up the uninvited guest in the tent.
Matted hair, a filthy face, clothes in rags—he looked for all the world like a mud-caked sack of scraps. The table was a shambles; it had plainly been ransacked.
'Stay back!'
The outlaw's fingers, clenched around the hilt, were withered and blackened, black crystals clinging to them.
She ought to have been frightened—but she saw the sheriff's hand hanging naturally at her side, the revolver only inches away.
Only last month she had come face to face with a manglerbeast out in the wilds, and by the time she understood what was happening, the thing had already lunged at her.
But at the crack of a single shot the manglerbeast dropped to the ground, and all she saw was the sheriff sliding the gun back into its holster before stepping forward and gathering her into her arms.
So she was not afraid. She knew the sheriff could deal with the man in front of them exactly as she had dealt with that manglerbeast, at any moment.
Yet the sheriff made no move at all.
'Do you... like chocolate?'
'...What?'
'The children and I are fond of it too. Whenever a caravan comes through, we buy some. Though... the water in that pot has gone cold by now, hasn't it? It tastes better hot.'
She followed the direction of the sheriff's pointing finger. On the ransacked table, a single ceramic cup stood perfectly upright, and beside it lay a wrapper torn open in haste.
'There'll be grilled meat and beer at the camp tonight. And hot chocolate too, of course. Perhaps... you'd care to join us?'
She heard the sheriff say it.

That night, the unfamiliar face appeared beside the campfire.
'How do you know he isn't a bad man?'
'I don't. That's why I'll be keeping a close eye on him.'
'But Mom says there are lots of bad people out in the frontier...'
'There are people who need help out here, too. Harsh weather, scarce supplies, all manner of venomous creatures and beasts... surviving in the frontier is that hard. Everyone is frightened, everyone is uneasy, and so they all race one another to pick up a weapon.'
The sheriff stroked her hair.
The sheriff had once knelt to close the eyes of that fallen manglerbeast, and the look in them then was the very same as the look in them now.
'Sometimes there truly is no other way. But at least here and now, as far as it lies within my power... I would like a cup of hot chocolate to work better than a bullet.'
In the end the girl went back to the campfire, still only half-convinced.
The man who 'might or might not be bad' huddled in a corner at first, cleared the food from his plate like a gale sweeping away clouds, and glared at everyone who turned a startled or wary look his way. Later, though, when the others began to sing, she noticed him listen for a while and then, of all things, start humming along under his breath.
I drifted all this way alone, without a coin to my name ♪
My hometown lies behind me, a thousand miles away ♪
